extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, literary critics, and students/scholars of poetry and drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for composing and judging poetry—especially tragic drama—based on Aristotle's Poetics (as edited/translated by S. H. Butcher). Covers fundamental concepts (mimesis), genre distinctions, the six elements of tragedy, rules for plot, character, diction, and answers to critical objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis) as the principle of the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and related arts are modes of imitation (mimesis); they represent life and action rather than merely record facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation underlies poetry, music, dance, painting, etc.; evaluation should ask how well a work imitates its objects according to its medium, objects, and manner of imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium (vehicle) by which imitation is effected: rhythm, language, and harmony (melody), taken singly or combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate medium(s) for the genre (e.g., epic privileges narrative language and metre; tragic drama employs language, rhythm, and harmony via dialogue, music, and choral song). Assess whether rhythm/language/melody are used effectively and not in conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation (types represented)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects imitated may be higher or lower types; difference of object is the basis for distinguishing genres such as tragedy and comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the chosen objects (characters, actions) are appropriate in moral/ethical 'height' to the genre (e.g., tragedy deals with serious/higher types). Misfit between object and genre is a flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner (form) of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may take several forms: dramatic (acted), narrative, or mixed; the manner of imitation (how the story is conveyed) is a defining criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the work functions best as drama, narrative, or lyric; mixing forms must be judged for organic unity rather than mere eclecticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological and historical origins (instincts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry arises from the instinct of imitation and from the human instinct for rhythm and harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to understand audience responses; works that appeal to these instincts (through vivid imitation, rhythmic/music qualities) produce stronger effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate a tragedy ask whether it presents a coherent, serious action with appropriate scale (neither trivial nor diffusely long).

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent elements of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy comprises six elements: Spectacle (opsis — presentment), Song (melos — lyrical element), Diction (lexis), Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), and Thought (dianoia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess each element; Aristotle ranks them with Plot as primary, then Character and Thought; Spectacle and Song are external/accessory but relevant when well integrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot (the representation of action) is of primary importance in tragedy; character and thought follow in importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the structure, causal coherence, and completeness of the plot first; a strong plot can compensate for weaker others, but a weak plot undermines the whole work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as a Whole (completeness and magnitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be a whole — complete in itself — with a beginning, middle, and end, and of adequate magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that incidents form a coherent whole that achieves a single integrated effect; size should be sufficient to produce that effect but not unnecessarily long.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (not unity of hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot consists in unity of action: the parts must be organically connected to one central action, not merely united by one protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject episodic or disconnected sequences that do not contribute to the central action; judge scenes by their necessity to the main action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic (universal) truth vs. historical truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry expresses universals; it speaks of what generally or typically happens, not isolated particular facts as history does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions and characters for their embodiment of universal truths (typical human motives and necessities) rather than strict factual accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of probable or necessary sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents must follow by probability or necessity; events should be arranged so that each incident leads naturally to the next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess causal links and logical necessity/probability between incidents; avoid arbitrary jumps that violate plausible sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of the inevitable and the unexpected
rubrics_metrics.description: The best tragic effects arise from a balance of what is inevitable and what is unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot should strive to surprise the audience while remaining consistent with what has been made probable or necessary—surprises must feel earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of plot: simple and complex
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple plots involve change without reversal/recognition; complex plots involve reversal (peripeteia), recognition (anagnorisis), and suffering (pathos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence and articulation of reversal and recognition; complex plots that integrate these elements can produce stronger tragic effects when properly motivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sudden change in the protagonist's situation from one state to its opposite, properly motivated within the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversals should be causally grounded and arise from the plot's actions, not from arbitrary contrivances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change from ignorance to knowledge—recognition—about persons or circumstances that transforms understanding within the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition scenes should be credible and integrated into the causal structure; they may be variously constructed but must be believable in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffering (pathos) as tragic incident
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that arouse pity and fear—suffering and painful incidents—are central to tragic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether pathos arises from the plot's necessities and the characters' choices, not from melodramatic excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of tragedy (structural segments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy has parts such as Prologue, Episodes, Choral Odes, and Exodus (and other quantitative divisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the placement, proportion, and function of these parts; avoid superfluous or ill-placed episodes that break unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes tragic action (change and character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic action involves a change of fortune, often due to character; the hero's moral purpose and its alteration are requisites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how the hero's decisions/character traits produce the change of fortune; the change should feel inevitable or highly probable given those traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for unhappy ending as truly tragic
rubrics_metrics.description: An unhappy ending more truly achieves tragic effect than a conventional 'poetic justice' preferred by popular audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge a tragedy inferior simply for an unhappy ending; assess whether the ending arises naturally from the action and achieves catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arousal and purgation of pity and fear (catharsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should arouse pity and fear, and through this bring about a purgation (catharsis) of such emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the audience's emotions are appropriately engaged and resolved by the end of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (opsis) subordinate to poetic aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacular effects (staging, scenery) are external and can work against the spirit of tragedy if they dominate the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spectacle as an adjunct that supports the plot and emotions; avoid relying on spectacle to substitute for poetic structure and character motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ethos) as manifestation of moral purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Character shows the moral purpose; ethical portraiture requires consistency, probability, and appropriate motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge characters for unified ethical purpose, credible motivations, and actions that conform to probability or necessity; depraved traits are permissible only if inner necessity justifies them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to deus ex machina
rubrics_metrics.description: Arbitrary devices (deus ex machina) that resolve the plot without organic necessity are censured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid solutions or reversals that come from outside the plot's causal logic; endings should flow from established actions and recognitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rules for the tragic poet (composition techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical advice: place the scene before the eyes and act parts to enter into the characters; sketch a bare outline of action before filling episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work from an outline of action to ensure unity; use embodiment/acting techniques to develop believable characters and dialogue; episodes should fill the planned skeleton, not distract from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful handling of complication and dénouement
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful about the complication (knots) and the dénouement (unraveling) of the plot, especially the denouement's plausibility and necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The complication and resolution must be proportionate and logically bound to prior incidents; avoid rushed or forced dénouements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of choral odes and varied poetic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Choral odes and lyrical elements should be organic parts of the whole; if possible, unite varied forms of poetic excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choral passages must advance or reflect the action and theme; avoid inserting choruses as decorative interludes unconnected to plot or emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) as intellectual element revealed in speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (the intellectual element) appears in dramatic speeches and should follow rhetorical rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the reasoning, thematic propositions, and rhetorical structure of speeches; thought should be coherent, persuasive, and relevant to action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis) and poetic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction (language) pertains to the art of delivery; poetic diction involves admissible words and modes of speech, including metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate word choice, figures of speech (esp. metaphor), level of language and appropriateness to character and genre; diction should combine elevation with clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevation with perspicuity in language
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should combine elevated language with perspicuity—high style must remain comprehensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscurity for its own sake; grand expressions should still convey meaning and support the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between Epic and Tragic modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic and Tragedy share unity of action but differ in length, metre, and the art of rendering implausible events plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing, attend to scale: epics allow greater length and breadth while tragedies aim for concentrated effect; judge plausibility strategies appropriate to each form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of improbability and impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A probable impossibility (an impossible thing made credible by art) is preferable to an improbable possibility; poetic plausibility can justify departures from common reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an apparently impossible element is artistically justified and coherent within the poem's established assumptions; prefer imaginative but consistent departures over random improbabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for examining contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent contradictions should be resolved by dialectical rules: check whether the same thing is meant in the same relation and sense; refer to what the poet implicitly or explicitly assumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique contradictions by interpreting authorial intent and the sensible assumptions of an intelligent audience rather than by literal literalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censure of irrational elements or depravity without necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational acts or morally depraved character traits are rightfully censured if introduced without an inner necessity within the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that problematic actions or traits be motivated by the plot's internal logic; arbitrary moral ugliness is a defect unless artistically required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and refinement considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Different genres address different audiences: epic is for a cultivated audience that does not need gesture, tragedy for a broader audience; but defects often lie with performers rather than the poetic form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating performance-dependent aspects (gesture, spectacle), separate poetic composition from histrionic execution; judge whether the work itself requires or tolerates such performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic end: produce the pleasure proper to the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Each art should produce the particular pleasure proper to it; tragedy's concentrated effect is often more pleasurable than a diluted effect spread over long time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work achieves the distinctive pleasure (e.g., intense, concentrated catharsis for tragedy) appropriate to its art, rather than merely producing generic entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of music and spectacle as accessory elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Music, choral song, and spectacle are important accessories but must be used to support the poetic whole, not replace it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether music and spectacle enhance the plot's unity and emotional aim; excessive or irrelevant musical/spectacular elements are faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre and technical craft (including handling of metres)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in metre distinguish genres (e.g., epic metre vs. tragic metres), and the poet must master technical metrical craft to impart plausibility and artfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate metre for appropriateness, skillful use, and contribution to the poem’s tone and pace; poor metrical choices can weaken plausibility and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering critical objections under enumerated heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical objections to poetry fall under five (or twelve expanded) heads—impossible, irrational, morally harmful, contradictory, and contrary to artistic correctness—and should be answered according to the treatise's principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Aristotle's taxonomy when responding to criticisms: show poetic justification (poetic truth, inner necessity, probability rules) rather than mere defense of bad art.
